issues.legal_issue: A later rent-control law’s modification of the rules for striking out a tenant’s defence applies to a pending eviction proceeding under the repealed law when the later law requires the court to have regard to its provisions.
material_facts: The eviction suit was pending under the 1952 Act when the 1958 Act came into force.
The former law required the court to strike out the defence upon the tenant’s failure to make a required rent payment or deposit.
The later law made striking out the defence discretionary rather than mandatory.
The tenant paid the overdue rent after the payment deadlines but before the application to strike out the defence was decided.
issues.conclusion: The court was required to apply the later law’s discretionary approach and consider the circumstances, including the tenant’s subsequent payment; it was not bound to strike out the defence merely because payment was late.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 57(2) of the 1958 Act, the direction that a court have regard to that Act means that modifications or clarifications of the former law are to be applied in pending proceedings. Karam Singh Sobti v. Pratap Chand governs that interpretation. Comparing Section 13(5) of the 1952 Act with Sections 15(1)–(7) of the 1958 Act, the Court held that Section 15(7)’s change from mandatory to discretionary striking out was a modification to be applied to the pending suit.

predicates.pending_eviction_proceeding_under_repeal: An eviction proceeding remained pending under an earlier rent-control law when a later rent-control law came into force.
predicates.later_law_requires_regard_to_its_provisi: The later law directs the court to have regard to its provisions when deciding the pending proceeding.
predicates.later_law_makes_striking_out_discretiona: The later law allows, but does not require, the court to strike out a tenant’s defence for failure to make a required rent payment or deposit.
predicates.tenant_later_paid_overdue_rent: The tenant paid rent after the required payment deadlines but before the application to strike out the defence was decided.

issues.definition: When a pending eviction proceeding is governed by a direction to consider a later law that makes striking out discretionary, and the tenant later pays the overdue rent, the court must consider whether to strike out the defence.

issues.legal_issue: A court’s failure to perform a statutory duty to apply relevant law means that the proceeding was not conducted according to law and may warrant revisional intervention.
material_facts: The trial court struck out the tenant’s defence, and the appellate court affirmed that order.
Neither court considered the later law’s discretionary rule, although the transition provision required regard to that law.
The tenant sought revision, and the High Court summarily dismissed the application.
The tenant’s overdue rent had been paid before the application to strike out the defence was decided.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have exercised its revisional power, set aside the orders striking out the defence, and rejected the landlord’s application to strike it out.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35 of the 1952 Act permits the High Court to examine whether a decision is according to law. Under Hari Shankar v. Girdhari Lal Choudhury, that inquiry concerns the decision as a whole and is not confined to errors of law or fact simpliciter. Where the law requires a court to have regard to specified provisions and it fails to do so, the proceeding is not according to law and may be corrected in revision.

predicates.revision_against_order_in_pending_rent_p: A party seeks revision of an order made in a pending rent-related proceeding.
predicates.court_failed_to_apply_law_it_was_require: The court deciding the proceeding did not consider law that it was legally required to take into account.

issues.definition: When revision is sought in a pending rent-related proceeding and the deciding court failed to apply law it was required to consider, the revisional court must correct that failure.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s failure to draw the court’s attention to a clear legal requirement does not excuse the court’s failure to comply with it.
material_facts: The courts below did not consider the transition provision requiring them to have regard to the later law.
It was suggested that counsel had not drawn the courts’ attention to that provision.
issues.conclusion: The omission by counsel did not justify the High Court’s refusal to intervene in revision.
issues.legal_principle: The court remains responsible for following clear provisions of law even when counsel does not raise them. The failure to comply with a statutory duty is not excused by counsel’s omission and may support revisional intervention under Section 35 of the 1952 Act, consistently with the approach in Hari Shankar v. Girdhari Lal Choudhury.

predicates.court_had_a_clear_legal_duty: The law clearly required the court to take a specified legal requirement into account.
predicates.court_failed_to_perform_that_duty: The court did not comply with that legal requirement.
predicates.counsel_did_not_raise_the_requirement: The parties’ counsel did not draw the court’s attention to the legal requirement.

issues.definition: When a court had a clear legal duty, failed to perform it, and counsel did not raise the requirement, counsel’s omission does not excuse the court’s failure.
